passage:
I've shared a hostel room with Chetan for two years, so I saw this unfold. In September I lent him a library book on rainwater harvesting. He read it in one night, underlining like mad.
In November he came back from his seminar glowing. "Sir loved my idea! Rooftop tanks linked to the school toilets. Totally mine." That was chapter four of the book, almost exactly, diagram and all. I'd read it too.
I said, "Isn't that from the book I lent you?" He looked genuinely puzzled, then pale. He dug out the book, found chapter four and sat down on his bed.
I don't think he was cheating; he looked too shocked for that. He emailed his professor that night to add the reference.
Saurabh

qa.q: Which chapter of the book matched Chetan's seminar idea?
qa.a: Chapter four of the book matched it almost exactly, diagram and all.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel the idea was "totally mine"?
qa.a: Chetan felt proud and excited, because he had absorbed the book two months earlier, so the idea came back feeling like his own thought, with its source forgotten.

qa.q: What did Chetan choose to do after finding chapter four, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He emailed his professor that night to add the reference, fixing the credit honestly before it became a bigger problem.

qa.q: How does Saurabh read Chetan's reaction?
qa.a: Saurabh thinks Chetan wasn't cheating because he looked genuinely puzzled and shocked, though Saurabh can only judge from his face.

grounding: It shows a roommate watching a male student present an idea from a borrowed book as his own because the source had faded.

passage:
Monday: In the canteen, Sumit tells Mridul his idea for their marketing assignment: a bike-sharing survey run in the canteen queue. Mridul nods, half-listening, eating his dosa.
Two weeks later: Mridul submits his proposal. The core idea, surveying students in the canteen queue about bike sharing, sits proudly in his introduction. He believes it came to him on the bus.
The following Friday: Sumit reads the proposal on the notice board and goes quiet. "That's my canteen idea, from the Monday we had dosas." Mridul starts to argue, then remembers: the dosa, the table, Sumit's hands drawing a queue in the air. His ears go hot.
That evening he writes to the professor, adding a line that credits Sumit, and the next Monday he buys Sumit a dosa.

qa.q: Where did Sumit first tell Mridul the idea?
qa.a: In the canteen on a Monday, while Mridul was eating his dosa.

qa.q: Why did Mridul believe the idea came to him on the bus?
qa.a: Mridul felt proud of the idea, because he was half-listening when Sumit shared it, so its source faded and later it surfaced feeling like his own.

qa.q: What did Mridul do once he remembered, and why was it the right step?
qa.a: He wrote to the professor that evening crediting Sumit, correcting the record openly instead of defending a mistake.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt reading the proposal on the notice board?
qa.a: Sumit probably felt hurt and unsure whether Mridul had taken it on purpose, which is why Sumit went quiet before speaking. 😔

grounding: It shows a male student who submits a friend's idea believing it was his own, until the lost source comes back.

passage:
Francis, you're writing your first big essay, so let old Samir uncle tell you something from my college days.
I was twenty and wrote a paper on village markets. There was one line I was very proud of: "A market is a newspaper you can eat." My professor circled it and wrote, "Beautiful. Whose is it?" I was offended. It was mine, I thought.
Months later I reopened a book of essays my roommate had given me. There it was on page thirty, word for word. I had read it once, liked it and forgotten I'd ever read it. My mind kept the line and threw away the label.
I went to the professor and told him. He said, "Good. Now you know why we keep a source notebook." I've kept one ever since. Start yours today.

qa.q: What did the professor write beside Samir's line?
qa.a: The professor wrote, "Beautiful. Whose is it?"

qa.q: Why was Samir offended at first by the professor's question?
qa.a: He had read the line once, liked it and forgotten reading it, so it honestly felt like his own creation.

qa.q: What habit does Samir urge Francis to start, and why?
qa.a: A source notebook, so that when an idea returns later, its label is still there and credit goes where it belongs.

qa.q: How did the professor see Samir coming back to own up?
qa.a: The professor seemed pleased, treating it as an honest slip worth learning from and using it to explain the source notebook.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a student, he took a line from a book as his own because the source was lost.

passage: The hostel wifi died at 11:10 pm, fifty minutes before Manoj's urban studies essay was due. He had the draft saved offline and one strong line he loved: "A city is an archive of the people who arrived in it." He had thought of it, he was sure, while walking back from the station last week. Siddharth, borrowing his charger, read the screen over his shoulder. "Nice line. Isn't that from the book I lent you?" Manoj frowned. "No, it's mine. I remember thinking it." But the words came to him too smoothly. He pulled the book from under his pillow and flipped pages as the clock ticked. There it was on page 84, underlined in his own pencil. He laughed weakly, typed the reference by phone hotspot, and submitted at 11:56.

qa.q: On which page did Manoj find the line, and how was it marked?
qa.a: It was on page 84, underlined in his own pencil.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel when Siddharth asked about the line, and what shows it?
qa.a: Manoj felt sure and a bit defensive, frowning and saying "No, it's mine", then embarrassed, laughing weakly when he found it underlined on page 84.

qa.q: What was the key choice Manoj made under time pressure, and what could make it easier next time?
qa.a: He chose to check the book instead of trusting his memory; noting page numbers beside ideas as he reads would make that check quick even with a deadline.

qa.q: What would have changed if Siddharth had not glanced at the screen?
qa.a: Manoj would likely have submitted a borrowed sentence as his own without meaning to, and could have been accused of plagiarism.

grounding: The passage shows a student believing an idea from a borrowed book was his own until he traces its source, avoiding accidental plagiarism.

passage: In a Pune college studio, the design group huddled over one laptop. "Okay, my idea," Nikhil said, eyes bright. "A bus-stop bench that collects rainwater for the plants behind it. Came to me last night." Seema clapped. Leela didn't. She tapped the table. "Nikhil, I sketched that in the canteen in July. On a paper napkin. You took the napkin home, remember?" Nikhil opened his mouth to say no, and then a picture surfaced: a napkin with a blue pen drawing, folded in his wallet. His ears went red. "I swear it felt like I thought of it yesterday," he said. "I wasn't trying to take it." Seema said gently, "Then put Leela's name on the slide." He did, and added "concept by Leela" in bold.

qa.q: Where did Leela first sketch the bench idea?
qa.a: In the canteen in July, on a paper napkin.

qa.q: What was Nikhil feeling when the napkin picture surfaced, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and a little shocked; his ears went red and he rushed to say he wasn't trying to take it, because the idea had honestly felt new to him.

qa.q: Which choice after the mix-up worked well, and why?
qa.a: Putting "concept by Leela" in bold on the slide worked because it fixed the credit openly, before the project went further.

qa.q: If you were Leela, what would you want from Nikhil in that moment?
qa.a: Leela would probably want the credit made clear and some sign that Nikhil believed her, which is what the bold line on the slide gave.

grounding: The scene shows a student honestly believing a friend's idea was his own because he lost track of where it came from.

passage: In the engineering department's project review, Kishore presented his idea with real pride: using old bicycle wheels to build a low-cost water lifter for farms. The professor liked it. Afterwards, in the corridor, Vasudha, his lab partner, said quietly, "That was my idea. In the canteen, back in August." Kishore laughed. "No, I thought of it on the train home." But that night he scrolled back through their chat. August 14th, Vasudha: 'What if we used cycle wheels to lift water? My uncle's farm needs something cheap.' His own reply: 'Interesting.' He sat very still. He had truly believed the idea was his. The next morning he emailed the professor, explained what had happened, and asked for Vasudha to be named as co-originator. Then he apologised to her in person.

qa.q: What was the idea for the project?
qa.a: Using old bicycle wheels to build a low-cost water lifter for farms.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he found Vasudha's August message?
qa.a: Kishore felt shocked and ashamed, sitting very still, because he had truly believed the idea came to him on the train.

qa.q: What did Kishore do the next morning, and why was it right?
qa.a: He emailed the professor to explain and asked for Vasudha to be named as co-originator, then apologised to her in person.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt watching Kishore present the idea?
qa.a: Vasudha probably felt hurt and overlooked, which is why she raised it quietly in the corridor.

grounding: Shows a student sincerely presenting a friend's idea as his own because he lost track of where it came from.

passage:
Dear Kunal,
I owe you an apology and an explanation. The line in my blog post that everyone liked, 'A city is a promise made in concrete', isn't mine. It's yours. You said it on the terrace in March, after the architecture lecture, and I laughed and said it was brilliant. Then I forgot. Last week it came back to me while I was writing, and it felt like my own thought, as if it had just arrived. I only realised when my sister read the post and said, "Isn't that what Kunal always says?"
I've edited the post to credit you, and I'm telling the people who shared it. I'm also starting a notebook where I write down good lines and who said them, because clearly my memory keeps the idea and throws away the name.
Sorry, friend.
Chaitanya

qa.q: Where did Kunal first say the line?
qa.a: On the terrace in March, after the architecture lecture.

qa.q: How did the line feel to Chaitanya while writing?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt pleased, sure it was a fresh thought of Chaitanya's own that had just arrived, because memory kept the idea and lost Kunal's name.

qa.q: What steps did Chaitanya take after realising, and why are they good?
qa.a: Editing the post to credit Kunal, telling people who shared it, and starting a notebook of lines and who said them, so sources aren't lost again.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Kunal would likely feel respected and touched by the honesty, and perhaps amused at how memory works.

grounding: Shows a student using a friend's line as original because the source was forgotten, then crediting it.

passage: Arohi, you asked about the worst week of my master's. Here it is. I'm Hemant. Two weeks before submission, the university's plagiarism check flagged a whole paragraph in my literature chapter. I was furious. I had written that paragraph at two in the morning, from my own head, I was sure. Then my supervisor showed me the match: an old textbook I'd read in my second year, almost word for word. I didn't remember reading that page at all. I remembered the idea, and my memory had quietly filed it as mine. That was the most frightening part: I hadn't meant to copy anything. I rewrote the section, cited the book properly, and my supervisor accepted it. Now, whenever I read, I note the page number beside the idea. My memory keeps the thought; the notebook keeps the source.

qa.q: What did the plagiarism check flag?
qa.a: A whole paragraph in Hemant's literature chapter.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when the paragraph was flagged, and then on seeing the match?
qa.a: Hemant felt furious at first, sure the paragraph was original, then frightened on seeing it matched a textbook read years before.

qa.q: What habit did Hemant build, and why does it help?
qa.a: Noting the page number beside every idea while reading, so the notebook keeps the source even when memory loses it.

qa.q: How did Hemant's supervisor handle the flagged paragraph?
qa.a: The supervisor showed the match and accepted the rewritten section once the book was cited properly.

grounding: Shows a student who unintentionally copied a paragraph because memory kept an idea and lost its source.

passage:
Week one. At a group study session, Sumit's classmate Seema suggested using a timeline poster to explain the history project. Sumit nodded, then got distracted by his phone.

Week three. Sumit presented his plan to the professor: "I had this idea for a timeline poster." He meant it. The idea felt completely his.

Week four. Seema caught him after class, quiet but hurt. "That was my idea. At the study session."

Sumit stared at her. He tried to remember. Slowly, the scene came back: her notebook, her drawing of arrows. His face went hot.

That evening he emailed the professor: "The timeline idea came from Seema. I forgot where I got it." He started keeping notes of who suggested what.

qa.q: What did Seema suggest at the study session?
qa.a: Using a timeline poster to explain the history project.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when Seema said it was her idea?
qa.a: He felt shocked and embarrassed, because the idea had truly felt like his own.

qa.q: What did Sumit do to fix it, and what habit did he start?
qa.a: He emailed the professor to credit Seema and started keeping notes of who suggested what.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when Sumit presented the idea?
qa.a: Seema felt hurt, since her idea was presented as someone else's.

grounding: A student believes an idea is his own when it came from a friend, showing how lost sources lead to unintentional plagiarism.

passage:
Kamal, you're worried about citing sources in your thesis? Let your Asif mamu tell you something from my college days.

In my final year, I wrote an essay on village water systems. There was a line in it I was very proud of, about wells being "the memory of a village." I thought I'd made it up.

My professor called me in. He opened a book from the library and showed me the exact line, word for word. I had read that book months earlier and forgotten.

I was so ashamed I couldn't look at him. But he said, "This happens. Your mind kept the words and lost the address." After that I kept a small notebook for every quote and idea, with where it came from.

qa.q: What line was Asif proud of in his essay?
qa.a: About wells being "the memory of a village."

qa.q: How did young Asif feel when the professor showed him the book?
qa.a: He felt deeply ashamed and couldn't look at the professor, because he had honestly believed the words were his.

qa.q: What turning point changed Asif's habits?
qa.a: The professor's kind explanation led him to keep a notebook for every quote and idea with its source.

qa.q: How did the professor seem to view Asif's mistake?
qa.a: The professor saw it as an honest lapse, not cheating, and treated him kindly.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a student, he used a book's line believing it was his own, because the source was lost.

passage:
The assignment was due at midnight, and Hrithik's laptop kept crashing. He typed fast, retyping paragraphs from memory each time.

His friend Noor was on video call, helping him check references.

"This bit about 'learning as a spiral, not a ladder,'" she said. "That's good. Did you come up with that?"

"Yes. I think so."

Noor frowned. "That's from the recorded talk we watched in class. I remember."

Hrithik stopped. He couldn't remember the talk at all. But he searched the class materials, and there it was, the same words.

He felt a wave of panic. "I would've submitted that as mine."

With eight minutes left, he added the citation and hit send, hands still shaking.

qa.q: How many minutes were left when Hrithik added the citation?
qa.a: Eight minutes.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik feel a wave of panic?
qa.a: He realised he had nearly submitted someone else's words as his own without meaning to, and felt scared and embarrassed.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do to avoid this next time?
qa.a: He could note the source whenever he writes down a good line or idea, so it doesn't get lost.

qa.q: How might Noor feel after catching the line?
qa.a: Noor was probably relieved she noticed, and glad to help her friend avoid trouble.

grounding: Under deadline pressure, a student nearly submits an idea he believes is his own but actually came from a class talk.

passage: In the seminar room of his Bengaluru college, Siddharth presented his plan for the design project: rain gutters that double as planters along the hostel walls. "It came to me in the shower," he said, grinning, and the professor nodded, impressed. Zainab, in the second row, went very still. Three weeks ago, over cutting chai at the canteen, she had sketched exactly that on a paper napkin, and Siddharth had said, "Cute idea." After class she caught him in the corridor. "The planter gutters. The napkin? Canteen?" Siddharth blinked, and then his face fell. He could see the napkin now, her pencil lines. "I honestly thought it was mine," he said. "I'll tell Professor Rao today."

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when Zainab reminded him of the napkin?

qa.q: What should Siddharth do now, and what habit could prevent this?

passage: "Listen to this line," Rafiq said, reading from his laptop. "Cities are not built, they are bargained over." "Nice," said Nilesh from the other bed. "Where's that from?" "From me. It just came to me yesterday." "Hmm. Didn't we read that in the urban studies book last term? The blue one?" "No way. I'd remember." "Check page one, man. The opening quote." Rafiq pulled the blue book off the shelf and flipped it open. There it was, word for word, with the author's name under it. "Oh no," he said. "I really thought I made it up." "Happens to everyone. Just quote it properly." "My essay is due in two hours." "So add the citation. Takes one minute." "I feel like a thief." "You're not a thief. You're a guy who reads."

qa.q: Where was the line printed in the blue book?

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he found the line in the book?
qa.a: He felt dismayed and guilty, "like a thief", because he genuinely believed he had made the line up.

qa.q: What was the right fix, and why?
qa.a: Quote it properly with a citation before the deadline; losing the source was honest, but crediting it keeps the essay honest.

qa.a: Nilesh sees it as ordinary, not cheating; Nilesh calmly points to the book and reassures Rafiq that it happens to everyone who reads.

passage: Last semester I won the college pitch contest with an idea for passing textbooks from seniors to juniors. I was proud. I told everyone, even my mother, that it came to me on a night bus. Two months later I was clearing out old voice notes and found one from Gargi, from our first week of college: "What if seniors just passed their books down, like a library, but between people?" I sat on my bed and played it four times. I had no memory of hearing it, yet there was my own reply: "Hmm, maybe." I called Gargi that night, embarrassed, and told her. Now I keep a notes file where I write down who said what. I'm still Madhav, who pitched it, but I'm no longer the only one who thought of it.

qa.q: What did Madhav find among the old voice notes?
qa.a: A voice note from Gargi from the first week of college: "What if seniors just passed their books down, like a library, but between people?"

qa.q: How did Madhav feel after playing the voice note four times?
qa.a: Madhav felt stunned and embarrassed: there was no memory of hearing the idea, yet Madhav's own reply was on the recording.

qa.q: What habit did Madhav take up, and why does it help?
qa.a: A notes file recording who said what, so ideas keep their sources and honest credit is easy to give.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel when Madhav calls?
qa.a: Gargi may feel surprised and a little hurt at first, but also respected, because Madhav owned up to it.

grounding: A student believes a winning idea was their own until an old voice note shows it came from a friend.

passage:
Project supervisor's note, end of the Christmas term
Imran's final design report proposed a clever idea: using old bicycle wheels as pulleys for the village water lift. He presented it confidently as his own, and I believe he meant it.
In the viva, Jeevan, his project partner, looked uncomfortable. Afterwards Jeevan showed me a photo from their shared notebook in September: the same sketch, in Jeevan's handwriting, with "from the library book on rural tech, p. 84" written beside it.
When I showed Imran, he went pale. "I really thought I came up with it on the bus," he said. He wasn't defending himself; he looked shaken.
I asked him to add a line crediting the book and Jeevan's note before final marks. I've also started asking every group to keep a "where did this come from" column in their project logs.
Dr Kaul

qa.q: Where did the pulley idea first come from?
qa.a: From the library book on rural tech, p. 84, noted beside a sketch in Jeevan's handwriting.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when he saw the September note?
qa.a: He was shaken and embarrassed, going pale, because he truly believed he had come up with it on the bus.

qa.q: What did Dr Kaul ask every group to keep, and why does it help?
qa.a: A "where did this come from" column in their project logs, so sources are written down before they are forgotten.

qa.q: What was the viva like for Jeevan?
qa.a: Jeevan felt uncomfortable watching the idea presented as Imran's own, and chose to show the supervisor the notebook quietly rather than accuse anyone.

grounding: Shows a student who sincerely believes an idea was his own when it came from a book and a friend's notes.
